name: Nguna
confidence_why: Schütz 1969 describes only sentence-final pitch contours and, as Clark 2025 notes, never treats stress as such, which is all the phrasal coding rests on, whereas Clark 2025 (citing McClintock 1991's instrumental finding of a three-mora measure with greater intensity on its first mora) and Billington, Thieberger and Fletcher 2020 both read Nguna as having antepenultimate stress, so fixed antepenultimate word stress is the better-supported reading, though the one instrumental study, McClintock 1991, is known only through Clark's summary. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Schütz 1969.

new_statements.quote: Stress is strong in all the dialects and in Nguna -Tongoa it is rather irregular. It is the strong stress that has done much to differentiate the Efate dialects from those of the surrounding islands. The following are the observed facts for Nguna itself: ... 2. Words of two syllables are normally stressed on the first syllable ... 3. Words of more than two syllables (apart from any question of the affect of an added suffix) are rather irregular. ... (ii) In words of three syllables the stress is frequently on the first ... 4. Inflectional elements in general do not affect the original stress ... no instances of stress on a final syllable appear.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Nguna 'phrasal' from Schütz 1969 §1.1 (intonation contours keyed to the syllable count of the sentence-final word). Capell describes word-level stress for Nguna: strong, largely retained under inflection and in compounds, disyllables initial, trisyllables mostly initial (= antepenultimate), penultimate on a final vowel cluster, never final, with lexical irregularity in longer words and a possible vowel-sonority effect; only monosyllable stress and a pre-pausal 'advance' are utterance-conditioned. That is a different TYPE from 'phrasal' (hence contradicts), though his data are broadly compatible with the antepenultimate word-stress reading of Schütz p. 11 that Billington et…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell (for Nguna itself, and Nguna-Tongoa-Sesake generally): word stress is strong but 'rather irregular'. Monosyllables are stressed or not according to their syntactic position in the utterance; disyllables are normally stressed on the first syllable ('ana, 'mana, 'noa, 'ma:ma, 'rani); words of three syllables are 'frequently' stressed on the first (na 'vanua, na 'lorika, 'da:piri, 'anino) and longer words 'often' likewise ('sunoro, 'dodomi) but not always (nakoro'atelani, ta'kariki vs taka'lapa), where 'the comparative sonority or weight of the vowels seems to exercise an influence in the placing of the stress'; inflectional suffixes in general do not move the stress ('natu/na, na'lake/na); stress falls almost universally on the first member of a final vowel cluster (si'kai, wano'noe) and never on a final syllable. He treats stress as a property of the word (retained under suffixation and in compounds), not fixed by a single edge rule; the examples are predominantly initial = antepenultimate in trisyllables, penultimate before a final vowel cluster. These remarks are restricted to Nguna-Tongoa-Sesake; in the Efate dialects proper (Havannah Harbour, Erakor), which permit closed syllables, loss of final vowels 'may result in a final stressed syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Reduplications carry a weak stress on the first and a strong stress on the third syllable (nani'nani 'goat', soro'soro 'tell a lie', ma,raue'raue 'bring out'); compounds retain the original stresses with some weakening of those earlier in the word (sinisini'leo 'wicked', 'da:pa'savasa 'worship'), with marked (non-phonemic) whispered vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) possessive suffixes are 'uncertain': ma ta'ma/na 'his father' but 'natu/na taka'lapa 'his elder son'; 'in general, the stress was advanced in pause' (..'pano pu'nusi ta'manu 'go to my father') 'but even this is not a regular treatment'; (ii) the 3rd person object -a is enclitic and advances the stress by one syllable (e mari'tadodo'mi a 'he pitied him', e dumi'li a 'he kissed him', e maripunu'e a 'he killed it'); two identical vowels in juncture coalesce into a long vowel that attracts the stress ('na:ata < na ata, pu'su:su < pusu'usu) [passage bracketed/struck in pencil with the note that vowel length is not phonemic in Nguna but is in Efate]; the whole account applies only to Nguna-Tongoa-Sesake, not to the closed-syllable Efate dialects where final stressed syllables arise from vowel loss.
new_statements.identity_note: The MS covers the whole Nguna-Efate dialect chain (Nguna, Tongoa, Sesake, Makura, Havannah Harbour, Erakor, plus remarks on Mae/Mele Polynesian); the stress facts quoted are stated explicitly 'for Nguna itself' and said to apply to Nguna-Tongoa-Sesake (nort2836, North Efate/Nakanamanga), not to the Efate dialects proper (South Efate, erk).

readall_conflicts: The only listed work (Capell MS) could not be opened, so no conflict can be established from it. Among the secondary sources already held by the project there is a mild disagreement about how to describe Nguna prominence rather than where it falls: Clark 2025 (Te Reo, p. 309) says Schütz 1969b p. 10 'does not discuss stress as such in Nguna, but finds a falling intonation contour at the end of declarative sentences which places prominence on the antepenultimate syllable', and McClintock 1991 pp. 88-89 describes 'a three-mora measure preference' with greater intensity on the first mora, which Clark 'will consider.. as antepenultimate (V3) stress'; Billington et al. 2020 (JASA 147(4), p. 2831) simply report 'antepenultimate stress in Nguna (Schütz, 1969, p. 11)'. Capell (per Billington 2020) speaks of 'strong stress' in the Efate dialects and of final prominence in varieties with many closed final syllables, which would apply to Nafsan/South Efate rather than Nguna. Capell's MS treats Nguna stress as word-level and 'rather irregular' (disyllables initial; trisyllables and longer words mostly but not always initial, i.e. antepenultimate in trisyllables; penultimate on a final vowel cluster; never final; suffixes generally do not shift it; enclitic object -a shifts it one syllable rightward), which conflicts in TYPE with the catalog's 'phrasal' coding taken from Schütz 1969's intonation section, while being broadly reconcilable with the antepenultimate word-stress reading of Sch…

sources.note: Schutz sets up no word-stress phoneme at all: pitch in Nguna is analysed as phrase-level intonation with three pitch levels, the phrase being delimited by pause. Two phrase-closing contours are word-length sensitive: /231/ when the phrase ends in a two-syllable word and /2311/ when it ends in a word of three or more syllables, i.e. the high pitch (/3/) falls on the antepenultimate syllable of a final word of 3+ syllables and on the penult of a final disyllable, and the same contours are heard on words spoken in isolation, which he says is what earlier descriptions had reported as 'antepenultim

sources.quote: Vowel length is contrastive in Nguna (Schütz 1969b:18-21), and probably in other dialects, though this is not yet clearly confirmed from my data.
